faqs.question: My sprinkler system is spraying water everywhere and won't stop. What do I do?
faqs.answer: Immediate steps: 1) Locate your main irrigation shutoff valve (usually near the backflow preventer or where the irrigation line branches from your main water supply). 2) Turn the valve clockwise to shut off water to the irrigation system. 3) If you can't find the irrigation shutoff, you can shut off your home's main water supply as a temporary measure. Once water is off, you can assess whether it's a broken head (easy fix) or a more serious mainline break.

faqs.question: Water is flooding my yard but I don't see a broken sprinkler head. What's happening?
faqs.answer: This typically indicates an underground leak, either in the mainline or a lateral line. Signs include: saturated soil with no visible water source, water bubbling up from the ground, and continuously soggy areas. Shut off water to the irrigation system and schedule a professional assessment. Underground leaks can waste thousands of gallons before they're obvious.

faqs.question: My basement/crawlspace is getting water and I think it's from the sprinkler system. Help!
faqs.answer: 1) Immediately shut off the irrigation system at the main valve. 2) If water is actively entering, consider shutting off your main home water supply. 3) Document the damage with photos. 4) Contact a professional for leak detection. Underground irrigation leaks can travel along pipes and emerge far from the actual leak location, making them difficult to trace.

faqs.question: My controller shows ERR or SHORT. What does this mean?
faqs.answer: ERR or SHORT typically indicates a wiring problem—either a short circuit in the valve wiring or a solenoid failure. First, turn off the controller. Then check for obvious wire damage (cut wires, exposed connections). You'll need a multimeter to test resistance (should be 20-60 ohms per solenoid). This is often a job for a professional with wire locating equipment.

faqs.question: My sprinkler system turned on during a freeze. What damage should I expect?
faqs.answer: Immediately shut off the system and assess: check for cracked pipes, broken heads, and split valves. Freeze damage often doesn't show up until you try to use the system again. Don't attempt repairs until temperatures are consistently above freezing. Document everything with photos for potential insurance claims. Professional assessment can identify hidden damage before it causes bigger problems.

faqs.question: I hit a sprinkler line while digging. How do I stop the gusher?
faqs.answer: Turn off the irrigation system immediately at the main valve. If you can't reach it quickly, shut off your home's main water supply. Once water is off, you can assess the damage. PVC pipe breaks are repairable—you'll need a coupling and primer/glue. If the break is on the mainline (the always-pressurized line), this requires immediate professional attention as it's wasting water even when the system isn't running.

faqs.question: My water meter is spinning fast but I don't see any leaks. What's happening?
faqs.answer: You likely have an underground irrigation leak. Turn off your irrigation system completely. If the meter stops spinning, the leak is in your irrigation system. If it continues, check indoor fixtures. Underground irrigation leaks can be substantial—even a small leak can waste 5-10 gallons per minute, adding hundreds of dollars to your water bill quickly.

faqs.question: Can a stuck valve cause my water heater to fail?
faqs.answer: No, irrigation and domestic water systems are separate. However, if your irrigation mainline has a leak, it can create pressure drops that affect your entire house water system. If you're experiencing both irrigation issues and water heater problems simultaneously, check your main water pressure—it may indicate a problem with your home's water service line, not the irrigation system specifically.

faqs.question: My backflow preventer is spraying water 20 feet in the air. What broke?
faqs.answer: This usually means the relief valve is stuck open or internal components have failed. Turn off the irrigation system immediately—this is wasting significant water. The relief valve is designed to dump excess pressure, but if it's constantly spraying, the backflow preventer needs repair or replacement. This typically requires a licensed professional as backflow devices must be tested and certified after repair.

faqs.question: Sprinklers are running but my controller says they're off. What's wrong?
faqs.answer: You likely have a valve stuck open. The controller sends electrical signals to valves, but if a valve diaphragm is stuck or damaged, water continues flowing regardless of electrical signals. Find the valve box for the zone that won't shut off and try manually turning the bleed screw or solenoid to close it. You'll need valve repair or replacement.

faqs.question: Water is pooling in my window well from my sprinklers. Emergency steps?
faqs.answer: Shut off the irrigation zone nearest to that area immediately. Redirect or adjust the heads that are spraying toward the window well. Window well flooding can lead to basement water damage quickly, especially in Denver's heavy clay soil that doesn't drain well. Consider installing shield deflectors on nearby heads or redesigning that zone to eliminate overspray.

faqs.question: My sprinklers are watering my neighbor's property. How do I fix this fast?
faqs.answer: Adjust the arc on the heads that are overspraying—most heads have an adjustment screw on top that you turn to reduce the spray pattern. If adjustment doesn't help, you may need different nozzles with a shorter radius or heads with built-in check valves to prevent low-head drainage. This is common on sloped properties in Denver areas like Highlands Ranch and Centennial.

faqs.question: When should I turn on my sprinkler system in Denver?
faqs.answer: Wait until the risk of hard freezes has passed, typically mid-April to early May in the Denver area. Watch the forecast—if temperatures will drop below freezing after startup, you may need to run water through the system briefly to prevent pipe damage, or delay startup. Mother's Day weekend is a traditional target date, but always check the 10-day forecast before scheduling startup.

faqs.question: What's the best time for sprinkler blowout in Denver?
faqs.answer: Schedule winterization between late September and mid-November. Don't wait for freezing weather—popular time slots fill up quickly. A hard freeze with water in your pipes can cause serious damage, so err on the side of earlier. Many Denver-area professionals recommend targeting the first week of October for scheduling, even though you may not actually need it until early November.

faqs.question: Can I run my sprinkler system in October in Denver?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as nighttime temperatures stay above freezing. Many Denver lawns benefit from continued watering into October, especially if fall has been dry. Just be prepared to winterize if a cold snap is forecast. October in Denver can swing from 70-degree days to sudden cold snaps, so watch the weather closely.

faqs.question: How do I protect my backflow preventer from freezing?
faqs.answer: Your backflow preventer should be drained during winterization. Some homeowners also wrap their backflow preventer with insulated covers during winter. The most important protection is professional winterization that removes all water from the device. Any water left inside can freeze and crack the brass body, requiring expensive replacement.

faqs.question: What's included in a professional spring startup?
faqs.answer: A professional startup includes: gradual system pressurization to prevent component shock, backflow preventer inspection, zone-by-zone testing of all heads, adjustment of misaligned heads, leak detection, controller verification and programming, and documentation of any issues found. This process identifies winter damage before it causes catastrophic flooding or high water bills.

faqs.question: How long should I wait after the last freeze to turn on my sprinklers?
faqs.answer: Wait at least 3-5 days after the last forecast freeze. Ground temperature is actually more important than air temperature—if there's still frost in the mornings, wait longer. In Denver, late April freezes are common, and starting too early can rupture pipes that are still brittle from cold soil temperatures. Patience saves money on freeze damage repairs.

faqs.question: Should I test all zones before adjusting my controller in spring?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Run each zone manually for 3-5 minutes before programming your automatic schedule. This reveals winter damage, broken heads, clogged nozzles, and pressure problems. Adjusting your controller without testing means you might be automatically watering with broken equipment, which wastes water and money. Make repairs first, then program.

faqs.question: Can I start one zone at a time over several days?
faqs.answer: Not recommended. When you pressurize the mainline for one zone, you're pressurizing the entire system. Any winter damage in other zones may start leaking even if those zones aren't running. It's better to test all zones in one session so you can identify all problems at once. Gradual startup doesn't reduce risk—it just delays finding problems.

faqs.question: What if I find a leak during spring startup?
faqs.answer: Shut off the system immediately and assess the damage. Small head leaks or cracked risers are quick fixes. Underground leaks or broken mainlines need professional attention. Don't ignore even small leaks—they waste hundreds of gallons per day and get worse over time. Spring is when most freeze damage reveals itself, so finding leaks early is normal.

faqs.question: When does Aurora Water allow spring irrigation startup?
faqs.answer: Aurora Water's watering restrictions typically begin May 1st. Before that date, there are no restrictions on testing and starting your system. Once restrictions begin, you can only water on assigned days. Check Aurora Water's current schedule—it varies by street address (odd/even) and can change based on drought conditions.

faqs.question: What PSI should be used for sprinkler blowout?
faqs.answer: Use 50-60 PSI for polyethylene (black flexible) pipe and up to 80 PSI maximum for PVC (white rigid) pipe. Never exceed 80 PSI—higher pressure can crack fittings and damage components. Most Denver systems use PVC mainlines and lateral lines. Professional blowout equipment includes regulators to prevent over-pressurization, which is why DIY with a small compressor often fails to fully clear the lines.

faqs.question: How many CFM does a compressor need for proper blowout?
faqs.answer: At minimum 80 CFM for most residential systems, though 100+ CFM is better for systems with multiple zones or large mainlines. A small 5-10 CFM home compressor can't move enough air volume to effectively clear water from pipes. This is why rental compressors or professional equipment is necessary—volume matters more than pressure for blowouts.

faqs.question: Can I damage my system with too much air pressure during blowout?
faqs.answer: Yes. Excessive pressure can crack pipe fittings, blow apart glued joints, damage backflow preventers, and rupture flexible hoses. Always use a pressure regulator. Signs of over-pressurization include loud banging sounds, fittings separating, or debris blowing out of heads. Professional blowout equipment includes safety regulators to prevent this.

faqs.question: Should I blow out zones individually or together?
faqs.answer: Always blow out zones individually. Running multiple zones simultaneously dilutes air pressure and volume across zones, leaving water in the pipes. Each zone should be blown out for 2 minutes, repeated 2-3 times per zone. The mist should transition from water spray to mostly air—when you see primarily air coming out, that zone is clear.

faqs.question: How do I know when a zone is completely cleared of water?
faqs.answer: The spray from heads transitions from solid water stream to fine mist to mostly air. When you see primarily air (minimal mist) and hear the distinctive sound change from wet to dry air flow, that zone is clear. Run each zone for 2 minutes, turn off, wait 30 seconds, repeat. Most zones need 2-3 cycles to fully clear, especially zones at lower elevations.

faqs.question: Should I remove my backflow preventer for winter or leave it installed?
faqs.answer: Leave it installed but ensure it's completely drained. Professional winterization drains the backflow preventer by opening the test cocks and petcocks. Removing it creates potential for debris entry and requires reinstallation and testing in spring. Proper drainage and an insulating cover are sufficient protection for Denver winters.

faqs.question: What settings should my backflow preventer valves be in after blowout?
faqs.answer: After blowout: test cocks should be OPEN (perpendicular to pipe), isolation valves should be CLOSED, and drain valves should be OPEN. This configuration allows any residual water to drain and prevents pressure buildup from temperature changes. Many homeowners forget to close isolation valves, which allows water back into the system during winter temperature swings.

faqs.question: Can I irrigate in November in the Denver metro?
faqs.answer: It's risky. November overnight lows in Denver frequently drop below freezing. If you must water, do it manually during afternoon hours when temps are warmest, and immediately blow out the system afterward. Most professionals recommend completing winterization by early November at the latest. One freeze with water in the lines can cause thousands in damage.

faqs.question: How early is too early for spring startup in Denver?
faqs.answer: Anything before mid-April is risky. March and early April can have hard freezes in Denver—even after several warm days. The soil takes time to warm up, and cold soil temperatures mean pipes are still vulnerable to freeze damage. If you start too early and a freeze hits, you'll need to drain the system again or risk damage. Patience saves money.

faqs.question: What's the difference between spring startup and just turning on the system?
faqs.answer: Spring startup includes gradual pressurization, testing each zone, checking for winter damage, adjusting heads, verifying controller settings, and documenting issues. Just turning it on is like flooring the gas pedal on a cold engine—you risk blowing pipes that were already weakened by winter, flooding your yard from undetected leaks, and wasting water from broken components you don't know about yet.

faqs.question: Do I need to winterize if I have a frost-free backflow?
faqs.answer: Yes! Frost-free backflows prevent water in the backflow device itself, but water remains in all your lateral lines, valves, and heads downstream. Those components still need to be blown out. The term 'frost-free' is misleading—it only applies to the backflow preventer, not your entire irrigation system. You still need full winterization.

faqs.question: How late can I schedule fall blowout in Denver?
faqs.answer: Don't wait past early November. By mid-November, most companies are fully booked or have shut down for winter. More importantly, a sudden cold snap can freeze your system before your scheduled appointment. Late October is ideal timing—you get it done before the rush while weather is still reliably above freezing. Waiting until you see frost in the forecast is too late.

faqs.question: Should I adjust my watering schedule as fall approaches?
faqs.answer: Yes, gradually reduce watering as temperatures cool. By September, most Denver lawns need 20-30% less water than peak summer. By October, you may only need one watering per week. Overwatering in fall promotes shallow roots and fungal disease. Watch your grass—if it's staying wet for hours after watering, you're watering too much or too frequently.

faqs.question: Can I skip winterization if we have a mild winter forecast?
faqs.answer: No. Weather forecasts are unreliable beyond a few weeks, and it only takes one unexpected cold snap to freeze your pipes. Denver's weather is notoriously unpredictable—we've had November freezes followed by 70-degree December days, then sudden January deep freezes. One freeze with water in the lines costs far more than winterization. Don't gamble.

faqs.question: What should I do if there's a late freeze after I've started my system?
faqs.answer: If a freeze is forecast after startup, you have two options: 1) Run the system briefly (5-10 minutes all zones) to keep water moving through the pipes during the coldest hours, or 2) Do an emergency blowout to remove all water before the freeze. Option 1 works for light freezes (28-32°F). For hard freezes below 25°F, option 2 is safer. Check your 10-day forecast carefully before spring startup.

faqs.question: Why are my sprinkler heads not popping up in one zone?
faqs.answer: Common causes include: low pressure in that zone from a leak or closed valve, clogged heads from dirt and debris accumulation, buried heads that have sunk below soil level, or worn internal components binding the riser. Start by checking if the zone's valve is fully open and look for obvious leaks in that zone. Denver's heavy clay soil often causes heads to sink over time, especially in areas with ground settling.

faqs.question: Why is water still coming out of my sprinkler heads after the system turns off?
faqs.answer: This indicates a valve that isn't closing completely. Causes include: debris caught in the valve diaphragm, worn or damaged diaphragm, damaged valve seat, or faulty solenoid. A professional can usually repair this by cleaning or replacing the diaphragm. This problem gets worse over time and wastes water continuously, even when you think the system is off.

faqs.question: My sprinkler system worked fine last year but has low pressure this spring. Why?
faqs.answer: Possible causes: winter freeze damage to pipes or valves, debris accumulation in valves or heads over winter, mainline leak that developed over winter, or municipal water supply changes (less common). A spring startup inspection can identify the issue. Low pressure after winter is one of the most common complaints in Denver—often it's a cracked pipe or valve that wasn't obvious until the system was pressurized.

faqs.question: How do I find my buried sprinkler valve box?
faqs.answer: If you've lost track of a valve box: 1) Follow the wires from your controller—they lead to the valves. 2) Look for depressions or slightly different grass color in a line from the controller. 3) Use a metal detector to find the solenoid. 4) A professional with wire locating equipment can trace underground wires directly. Valve boxes often sink below grade in Denver's clay soil and get covered by grass over time.

faqs.question: One zone runs for a few seconds then stops. What's wrong?
faqs.answer: This often indicates a wiring problem or failing solenoid. Check: wire connections at the controller, inspect for damaged wires, test the solenoid resistance with a multimeter (should be 20-60 ohms), or look for a short circuit in the wiring. This specific symptom usually means the solenoid is getting power but can't hold it—often a sign of a failing coil or corroded wire connections.

faqs.question: How do I test if a solenoid is bad with a multimeter?
faqs.answer: Set your multimeter to resistance (ohms). Disconnect wires from the solenoid. Touch the probes to the two solenoid terminals. You should read 20-60 ohms for most residential solenoids. If you read infinite resistance (OL) or zero ohms, the solenoid is bad. Also test for shorts to ground by touching one probe to a terminal and one to the metal valve body—should read infinite.

faqs.question: What does it mean when my zone runs for 3 seconds then stops?
faqs.answer: This is usually a short circuit in the zone wiring or a failing solenoid. The controller sends power, the valve starts to open, but then the short trips the controller's overload protection. Check for: corroded wire connections, damaged wire insulation (look where wires exit the controller or near valve boxes), or a solenoid coil that's shorted internally. This is different from a valve that won't open at all—the brief run indicates power is getting through.

faqs.question: Why do some zones have strong pressure and others weak?
faqs.answer: Most common causes: leak in the weak zone draining pressure, too many heads on one zone exceeding capacity, partially closed valve, elevation differences (lower zones naturally have higher pressure), or mainline sizing issues. In Denver's hilly areas like Highlands Ranch, elevation changes can cause 5-10 PSI differences between zones. Pressure regulators may be needed on high-pressure zones.

faqs.question: How can I tell if the problem is electrical or hydraulic?
faqs.answer: Manually open the valve using the bleed screw or solenoid. If water flows normally, the problem is electrical (wiring or solenoid). If water doesn't flow or flows weakly, the problem is hydraulic (leak, clog, or failed diaphragm). This simple test saves diagnostic time. Most valve boxes have a manual on/off mechanism—usually a screw on top of the solenoid that you turn counterclockwise.

faqs.question: What causes a sprinkler head to rotate in only one direction?
faqs.answer: For gear-driven rotors, this usually means debris in the gear mechanism or worn gears. Try removing the top cap and flushing debris. If that doesn't work, the gear drive is likely worn and needs replacement. Impact rotors that stick are usually due to a worn spring or debris in the mechanism. Most rotor heads in Denver eventually need replacement due to hard water deposits affecting the gears.

faqs.question: Why is my rotor head clicking but not rotating?
faqs.answer: The clicking indicates the gear mechanism is trying to work but is jammed or the spring is broken. Common causes: debris in the gear housing (especially grass clippings and dirt), broken return spring, or worn gears. Remove the cap, flush debris, check for smooth rotation by hand. If gears are worn or plastic is cracked, replace the head. Clicking without rotation means the mechanism is attempting to work but physically can't.

faqs.question: What's causing a rainbow or misting effect in my spray pattern?
faqs.answer: Misting (water atomizing into fine droplets) is caused by excessive pressure. Spray heads are designed for 20-30 PSI; higher pressure atomizes the water, causing waste from wind drift and evaporation. Solutions: install pressure-regulating heads, add pressure regulators to the zone, or check if your water pressure is too high (over 60 PSI at the source). This is common in Denver areas with high municipal pressure.

faqs.question: How do I locate a buried valve box that I've lost track of?
faqs.answer: Start at the controller and follow the wire bundle—valves are typically 10-20 feet from the controller in a line toward the zones they control. Look for slight depressions in the grass or different grass color. Use a metal detector to find the solenoid. A professional wire locator can trace the wire path directly. Valve boxes in Denver often sink 2-3 inches below grade due to settling clay soil and need to be uncovered.

faqs.question: What tools do I need for basic sprinkler head replacement?
faqs.answer: For most head replacements: adjustable pliers or channel locks (to grip the riser), new head that matches your system, and potentially a new riser if the old one is damaged. You may also want plumber's tape for threaded connections and a small shovel to expose the riser. Head replacement is one of the easier DIY repairs—the key is making sure the new head is compatible with your existing nozzles and pressure.

faqs.question: Can I use my water meter to detect irrigation leaks?
faqs.answer: Yes. Turn off all water in your house (including ice makers, toilets, etc). Check the meter—if it's moving, you have a leak somewhere. Then turn off the irrigation system at its main valve. If the meter stops, the leak is in the irrigation system. If it continues moving, the leak is in your house plumbing. Even small irrigation leaks can waste 5-10 gallons per minute, showing up as a steadily spinning meter.

faqs.question: Why is one zone flooding while another is dry?
faqs.answer: The flooding zone likely has a leak or stuck-open valve draining pressure from the other zones. Turn zones on individually to isolate the problem. If the dry zone works fine when run alone but fails when other zones run, you have a mainline pressure or capacity issue. Denver systems with undersized mainlines often show this symptom when multiple zones try to draw water simultaneously.

faqs.question: What causes sprinkler heads to sink below grade?
faqs.answer: Denver's clay soil expands when wet and contracts when dry, causing ground movement. Over years, this settling pushes heads downward. Also, heavy foot traffic, mowers hitting heads, and poor installation can cause sinking. Pull heads up by excavating around them, add soil or gravel below for support, and ensure the head sits flush or slightly above grade. Consider swing joints for heads in high-traffic areas.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to replace a zone valve vs repair it?
faqs.answer: Valve repair (replacing diaphragm and cleaning) is usually sufficient and costs significantly less than full valve replacement. Full valve replacement is needed when the valve body is cracked, threads are damaged, or internal components are corroded beyond cleaning. Most valve problems in Denver are diaphragm or solenoid issues that don't require replacing the entire valve body. Our online scheduler shows current pricing.

faqs.question: Can I replace just the diaphragm or do I need a whole new valve?
faqs.answer: Most often you can replace just the diaphragm. Remove the top of the valve (usually 4-6 screws), clean everything inside, and install a new diaphragm. This solves 80% of valve problems. Full valve replacement is only needed if the body is cracked, threads are stripped, or internal ports are damaged. Always try cleaning and diaphragm replacement first—it's much cheaper and usually fixes the issue.

faqs.question: What's involved in repairing a broken lateral line?
faqs.answer: Locate the break (look for soggy areas or water surfacing), dig down to expose the pipe, cut out the damaged section with PVC cutters, clean and dry the pipe ends, apply PVC primer and cement, join with a coupling or slip-fix connector, backfill and test. Most lateral line breaks are straightforward DIY repairs if you can access the pipe. Mainline breaks (always under pressure) are more urgent and often need professional repair.

faqs.question: How do professionals locate underground wire breaks?
faqs.answer: Professionals use specialized wire locating equipment that sends a signal through the wire and detects where it stops. They can trace the wire path from controller to valve and identify the exact point where the signal disappears—that's where the break is. DIY methods (following wires visually, testing with multimeter) work but are time-consuming. Denver's rocky soil often causes wire damage during ground settling.

faqs.question: What's the typical cost to repair freeze damage in spring?
faqs.answer: Freeze damage varies widely—anywhere from a few broken heads (relatively inexpensive) to cracked mainlines and split valves (much more costly). Most Denver systems with proper winterization don't have freeze damage. If you skipped blowout, expect multiple issues: cracked pipes, split fittings, damaged backflow preventers, and broken valve diaphragms. Prevention through proper winterization is far cheaper than spring freeze damage repair.

faqs.question: Can broken PVC be repaired or must it be replaced?
faqs.answer: Small cracks can sometimes be repaired with couplings or repair sleeves. Large breaks, shattered sections, or cracks near fittings require cutting out the damaged section and replacing it. PVC repair is straightforward: cut out the bad section, use a coupling or slip-fix, prime and cement, test. The repair is often stronger than the original pipe. Denver's temperature swings can make older PVC brittle over time.

faqs.question: How long do sprinkler repairs typically take?
faqs.answer: Simple repairs (head replacement, nozzle cleaning) take 15-30 minutes. Valve repairs take 30-60 minutes. Wire repairs depend on accessibility—anywhere from 1 hour if the break is obvious to several hours if extensive locating is needed. Pipe repairs vary by depth and accessibility. Most service calls identify multiple small issues that add up. Complex repairs may require return visits for parts.

faqs.question: Should I upgrade components when repairing or use original specs?
faqs.answer: If the original components worked well, replacement with equivalent parts is fine. However, consider upgrades if: you want better water efficiency (MP Rotator nozzles instead of standard spray), you have pressure problems (pressure-regulating heads), or the original parts are discontinued. Upgrading one zone at a time during repairs is a smart way to gradually improve efficiency without doing a full system overhaul.

faqs.question: What's the lifespan of a repaired valve vs new valve?
faqs.answer: A properly repaired valve (new diaphragm, cleaned internals) should last another 5-10 years. A new valve typically lasts 15-20 years. The valve body itself rarely fails—it's the internal moving parts (diaphragm, seals) that wear out. If the valve body is cracked or corroded, replacement is necessary. But most valve issues are resolved with a $10 diaphragm kit rather than a $60+ full valve replacement.

faqs.question: How do professionals locate underground leaks?
faqs.answer: Professionals use a combination of: visual inspection (wet spots, lush grass, surface water), pressure testing (isolate zones and monitor pressure drop), acoustic listening devices (detects water under pressure), and tracer wire following. Denver's heavy clay soil can hide leaks—water travels along pipes and surfaces far from the actual break. Thermal imaging can sometimes detect temperature differences from underground water flow.

faqs.question: Can I fix a leak by wrapping it with tape?
faqs.answer: No. Pipe tape and sealants are temporary at best and often fail under pressure. PVC repair requires cutting out the damaged section, cleaning the pipe, and using proper primer and cement with a coupling. Anything pressurized (mainline, laterals when zones run) will blow through tape quickly. Tape is only appropriate for very temporary emergency measures until you can make a proper repair.

faqs.question: Why does my lawn have dry spots even though my sprinklers run regularly?
faqs.answer: Common causes: heads clogged with debris reducing spray distance, heads sunken below grade can't pop up fully, pressure problems causing weak spray, heads misaligned or blocked by plants, or your zones don't provide overlapping coverage. Walk through during watering to observe—dry spots are often caused by heads that used to reach that area but have lost pressure or gotten clogged over time.

faqs.question: How much should I water my lawn in Denver?
faqs.answer: Most established Denver lawns need about 1 inch of water per week during summer, including rainfall. This typically translates to 2-3 watering days per week during peak summer, less frequent watering in spring and fall, and adjustment based on actual rainfall. Overwatering is as common as underwatering and wastes money while promoting shallow roots. Use the screwdriver test—soil should be moist 6 inches deep after watering.

faqs.question: What is the best time of day to water my lawn in Denver?
faqs.answer: Water between 4 AM and 10 AM. Early morning watering reduces evaporation loss (Denver's dry air and intense sun can evaporate 50% of midday water before it soaks in) and gives grass blades time to dry before nightfall. Watering at night keeps grass wet for hours, which promotes fungal disease. If your controller supports it, set start times in the pre-dawn window for the best results.

faqs.question: What is the cycle and soak method, and should I use it in Denver?
faqs.answer: Cycle and soak means splitting your watering into shorter intervals with breaks in between, allowing water to absorb before applying more. For example, instead of running a zone for 20 minutes straight, you run it for 7 minutes three times with 30-minute breaks. This is especially important in Denver where clay soils absorb water slowly and slopes cause runoff. Most smart controllers have a built-in cycle and soak feature.

faqs.question: How do I know if I'm overwatering my lawn?
faqs.answer: Signs of overwatering include spongy or mushy turf when you walk on it, mushrooms growing in the lawn, a persistent thatch layer, yellowing grass (not from drought but from root rot), and puddles that linger hours after watering. Overwatering is extremely common in Denver because people assume the dry climate means more water is always better. If your soil is wet 24/7 at 3-4 inches deep, you're overwatering.

faqs.question: What are the signs of underwatering my lawn in Denver?
faqs.answer: Classic underwatering signs include grass blades folding or curling inward, a blue-gray tint instead of bright green, footprints that stay visible for more than a few seconds after walking across the lawn, and soil that's hard and dry when you push a screwdriver into it. Denver's low humidity and intense UV stress grass quickly, so catching these signs early prevents permanent damage to your turf.

faqs.question: How do I do a screwdriver test to check soil moisture?
faqs.answer: Push a long screwdriver or soil probe into your lawn about 30 minutes after watering. It should slide in easily to a depth of 6 inches. If it stops or requires force, the water hasn't penetrated deep enough and you need to water longer or use the cycle and soak method. Check multiple spots across each zone since coverage can vary. This simple test is the most reliable way to know if your system is actually delivering enough water.

faqs.question: What watering schedule does Denver Water recommend?
faqs.answer: Denver Water's summer watering rules typically allow watering no more than three days per week during the irrigation season, with specific assigned days based on your address. Watering is prohibited between 10 AM and 6 PM from May through October. These rules can tighten during drought years, so check Denver Water's current restrictions each spring. Violating the rules can result in fines, so make sure your controller schedule is compliant.

faqs.question: What happens if I violate Denver Water's watering restrictions?
faqs.answer: Denver Water enforces a progressive penalty system. First offenses typically result in a warning notice, but repeat violations can lead to fines that increase with each occurrence. During severe drought, enforcement ramps up significantly. The easiest way to stay compliant is programming your controller to the correct assigned days and keeping watering times before 10 AM. A smart controller with weather adjustments makes compliance nearly automatic.

faqs.question: How do I adjust my sprinkler schedule for different seasons in Denver?
faqs.answer: Denver's watering needs change dramatically by season. In spring (April-May), water 1-2 days per week as temperatures climb. Peak summer (June-August) requires 2-3 days per week. Fall (September-October), taper back to 1-2 days. Shut down completely by late October for winterization. A good rule of thumb: your summer peak schedule uses roughly 2-3 times the water of your spring schedule. Smart controllers adjust this automatically based on local weather data.

faqs.question: Should I install a rain sensor on my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. A rain sensor is one of the cheapest and most effective upgrades for any irrigation system. It pauses your scheduled watering when it detects rainfall, preventing waste and keeping you compliant with Denver Water rules that prohibit watering during and after rain. Wired and wireless models are available, and they typically mount on a fence post or eave with a clear view of the sky. Most pay for themselves within one season through water savings.

faqs.question: What is evapotranspiration (ET) and why does it matter for my sprinklers?
faqs.answer: Evapotranspiration (ET) is the combined water lost through evaporation from the soil and transpiration from plant leaves. In Denver, ET rates are high due to our altitude, intense sun, low humidity, and frequent wind. Smart controllers use local ET data to calculate exactly how much water your landscape needs each day. Instead of guessing at run times, an ET-based controller waters precisely what your lawn lost, which typically reduces water use by 20-40%.

faqs.question: Why is my water bill so high during summer?
faqs.answer: Irrigation is the number one cause of high summer water bills in Denver. Common culprits include zones running longer than necessary, leaks in underground lines you can't see, a stuck valve that lets water flow continuously, schedules that weren't adjusted from peak summer settings, or heads spraying onto sidewalks and driveways. Start by checking your meter with the system off. If it's still spinning, you have a leak. If not, audit your zone run times and coverage.

faqs.question: How long should I run each sprinkler zone?
faqs.answer: Run times depend on the head type. Rotor zones (large rotating heads) typically need 25-40 minutes to deliver adequate water. Spray zones (pop-up fixed-pattern heads) apply water much faster and usually need only 8-15 minutes. Drip zones for beds may run 30-60 minutes. These are starting points for Denver clay soil. The real test is whether water penetrates 6 inches deep, so use the screwdriver test after watering and adjust up or down from there.

faqs.question: How do I water a sloped yard without causing runoff?
faqs.answer: Slopes are the biggest runoff challenge in Denver landscapes. Use the cycle and soak method: run the zone for short intervals (5-8 minutes) with 30-minute breaks between cycles to let water absorb. Point rotors uphill when possible so water flows back over already-watered areas. Consider converting steep slopes to drip irrigation or low-water plantings. If you see water running off the slope and onto sidewalks or streets, your intervals are too long.

faqs.question: How should I water new sod in Denver?
faqs.answer: New sod needs significantly more water than established turf for the first 2-3 weeks. Water 2-3 times daily for short durations (10-15 minutes per zone) to keep the sod and soil surface consistently moist while roots establish. After 2-3 weeks, reduce to once daily. By week 4-6, transition to a normal deep-and-infrequent schedule. The goal is to gradually encourage roots to grow deeper. Lift a corner of the sod periodically to check that it's moist underneath but not standing in water.

faqs.question: How do I water newly seeded areas with my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Seed needs the top inch of soil to stay consistently moist until germination, which takes 7-21 days depending on grass type. Run affected zones for 5-10 minutes, 3-4 times per day. Avoid heavy watering that puddles or washes seed away. Once grass reaches about 2 inches tall, reduce frequency to once daily and increase duration. Gradually transition to a normal deep watering schedule over the following 3-4 weeks as roots establish.

faqs.question: Does Kentucky bluegrass need more water than other grasses in Denver?
faqs.answer: Yes, Kentucky bluegrass (the most common lawn grass in the Denver metro) is one of the thirstier cool-season grasses, needing about 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week in peak summer. Tall fescue is more drought-tolerant and needs roughly 20% less water. If you're looking to reduce water use, consider overseeding with tall fescue or transitioning high-use areas to a bluegrass-fescue blend. Buffalo grass and blue grama need even less but have a different look and feel.

faqs.question: Can I water trees and shrubs with my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Sprinkler zones designed for lawns are not ideal for trees and shrubs because they deliver shallow, frequent water when woody plants need deep, infrequent soaking. The best approach is a dedicated drip zone for beds and tree rings, which delivers water slowly at root level without wetting foliage. If drip isn't an option, supplement with a slow-running hose at the drip line of each tree for 30-60 minutes every 1-2 weeks during summer. Newly planted trees need more attention than established ones.

faqs.question: How often should I water my trees during a Denver drought?
faqs.answer: Even established trees need supplemental water during Denver's periodic droughts. Water trees deeply every 2-4 weeks during dry periods, applying water slowly at the drip line (the outer edge of the canopy), not at the trunk. Newly planted trees need deep watering every 1-2 weeks. A soaker hose or drip ring is ideal. Denver's native trees are adapted to dry conditions but prolonged drought without supplemental water can stress even mature trees, making them vulnerable to pests and disease.

faqs.question: What water conservation tips work best for Denver irrigation systems?
faqs.answer: The biggest wins for Denver homeowners: install a smart controller that adjusts to weather automatically, fix leaks immediately (even small ones waste thousands of gallons), use the cycle and soak method on clay soil, add a rain sensor, water only before 10 AM, and make sure heads aren't spraying pavement. Converting low-use turf areas to xeriscape or drip-irrigated beds can cut your outdoor water use by 30-50%. Small changes add up fast at Denver's water rates.

faqs.question: Should I use a smart sprinkler controller in Denver?
faqs.answer: A smart controller is one of the best investments you can make for a Denver irrigation system. These controllers pull local weather data and adjust watering automatically based on temperature, rainfall, humidity, and wind. In Denver's highly variable climate (where you can get 80 degrees one day and snow the next), this prevents waste from watering before a storm or under-watering during a heat wave. Most homeowners see 20-40% water savings, which means the controller often pays for itself in 1-2 seasons.

faqs.question: How do I do a catch cup test to measure sprinkler output?
faqs.answer: Place 5-6 identical straight-sided containers (tuna cans work great) evenly throughout a zone. Run the zone for 15 minutes, then measure the depth of water in each container with a ruler. Multiply by 4 to get the hourly precipitation rate. Ideally, all containers should have similar amounts. If they vary wildly, you have a coverage or pressure problem. This test tells you exactly how long each zone needs to run to deliver 1 inch of water.

faqs.question: Why does Denver's clay soil make watering so difficult?
faqs.answer: Denver's heavy clay soil absorbs water very slowly, about 0.1 to 0.3 inches per hour, but most spray heads apply water at 1.5+ inches per hour. That mismatch means most of the water runs off before it can soak in. This is why cycle and soak is essential here. The upside of clay is that once water is absorbed, it holds moisture longer than sandy soil, so you can water less frequently. Short, repeated cycles are the key to working with Denver clay rather than fighting it.

faqs.question: How much water does a typical Denver lawn irrigation system use?
faqs.answer: A typical Denver metro home with a 5,000 square foot lawn uses roughly 30,000 to 50,000 gallons of water per irrigation season. That often represents 50-70% of your total annual household water use. Inefficient systems with leaks, overspray, or excessive run times can push that much higher. If your summer water bill is more than 3-4 times your winter bill, your irrigation system is likely using more water than necessary and an efficiency audit would help.

faqs.question: Can I water my lawn during a Denver drought restriction?
faqs.answer: During drought restrictions, Denver Water and surrounding districts typically reduce the number of allowed watering days rather than banning irrigation entirely. You can still water, but on a more limited schedule with stricter enforcement. Mandatory restrictions may limit watering to 2 days per week or even 1 day per week during severe drought. Check your specific water provider's current rules each spring, as restrictions vary by district across the metro area.

faqs.question: What's the difference between deep watering and frequent light watering?
faqs.answer: Deep watering means applying enough water to soak the soil 6-8 inches deep, then letting it dry out before watering again. Frequent light watering only wets the top inch or two, which trains grass roots to stay shallow and makes your lawn more vulnerable to heat and drought. In Denver, deep and infrequent watering is almost always better. Two or three thorough waterings per week will produce a healthier, more drought-resistant lawn than daily light sprinkles.

faqs.question: Should I adjust my sprinkler run times when it's windy in Denver?
faqs.answer: Yes, wind seriously impacts sprinkler efficiency. Denver regularly gets gusty afternoons that can blow spray patterns off target and accelerate evaporation. If possible, schedule watering for early morning when wind is typically calm. On unusually windy days, a smart controller with a wind sensor can delay watering automatically. If your system runs during high wind, you're wasting water and getting uneven coverage, especially with spray heads that are more affected by wind than rotors.

faqs.question: What are the different types of sprinkler heads used in Denver irrigation systems?
faqs.answer: The main types are spray heads, rotors, MP rotators, and drip emitters. Spray heads cover small areas with a fan of water and are great for narrow strips and small lawns. Rotors throw water in a rotating stream for larger turf areas, and MP rotators are a water-efficient hybrid that works well in Denver's windy conditions. Your system might use a mix of all four depending on your yard layout.

faqs.question: What pop-up height do I need for my sprinkler heads?
faqs.answer: Pop-up heights come in 2-inch, 4-inch, 6-inch, and 12-inch options, and the right choice depends on what the heads need to clear. For short-mowed lawns, 4-inch pop-ups are the Denver standard since they rise above typical bluegrass height. Use 6-inch or 12-inch in garden beds, ground cover, or anywhere vegetation might block the spray. Going too short means water hits the grass blades instead of spraying over them, which kills your coverage.

faqs.question: How do I choose the right sprinkler nozzle for my yard?
faqs.answer: Nozzle selection comes down to matching precipitation rates across each zone so water applies evenly. You want to pick nozzles based on the arc and radius needed for each head's location, making sure all heads on the same zone put out roughly the same inches per hour. Mixing spray nozzles and rotors on the same zone is a common mistake that leads to soggy spots and dry patches. If you're not sure what you need, check out 5280sprinklers.com to schedule a system evaluation.

faqs.question: What type of irrigation valves does my sprinkler system use?
faqs.answer: Most residential systems in Denver use electric solenoid valves that open and close when your controller sends a signal through the valve wire. These are typically globe-style or anti-siphon valves installed in underground valve boxes throughout your yard. When a valve fails, it usually either won't open (dead zone) or won't close (zone that runs forever and drives your water bill up). Valve replacement is one of the most common repairs we handle at 5280 Sprinklers.

faqs.question: Should I upgrade to a smart sprinkler controller in Denver?
faqs.answer: A smart controller is one of the best upgrades you can make for a Denver irrigation system. These Wi-Fi-connected timers adjust watering schedules automatically based on local weather data, which is huge when Denver swings from 90-degree heat to afternoon thunderstorms in the same week. Most homeowners see a 20 to 30 percent reduction in water use compared to a basic digital timer. Visit 5280sprinklers.com if you want to explore smart controller installation options.

faqs.question: What's the difference between mechanical and digital sprinkler timers?
faqs.answer: Mechanical timers use dials and pins to set watering schedules, while digital controllers use electronic programming with LCD screens. Mechanical timers are becoming rare because they lack flexibility and tend to drift over time, making them unreliable for Denver's watering restrictions. Digital controllers give you precise scheduling with multiple programs, and smart controllers take it a step further with weather-based adjustments. If you're still running a mechanical timer, it's probably time for an upgrade.

faqs.question: What is a backflow preventer and why does Denver require one?
faqs.answer: A backflow preventer keeps irrigation water from flowing backward into your drinking water supply, and Denver Water requires one on every sprinkler system. The most common types in the Denver metro are the PVB (pressure vacuum breaker), RPZ (reduced pressure zone), and DCA (double check assembly). Your property's specific setup depends on factors like elevation, whether you have an above-ground or below-ground installation, and local code requirements. Annual backflow testing is required by law, and 5280 Sprinklers handles testing and certification at 5280sprinklers.com.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a PVB and an RPZ backflow preventer?
faqs.answer: A PVB (pressure vacuum breaker) is the most common and affordable option for residential systems, but it must be installed at least 12 inches above the highest sprinkler head and cannot handle back pressure. An RPZ (reduced pressure zone) assembly is a more robust device that protects against both back-siphonage and back pressure, making it required for certain commercial and high-risk installations. RPZs also discharge water when they sense a problem, so they need to be installed where drainage is possible. If you're unsure which one your property needs, the team at 5280sprinklers.com can evaluate your setup.

faqs.question: What type of pipe is used in Denver sprinkler systems?
faqs.answer: Most Denver irrigation systems use PVC (white rigid pipe) for mainlines and lateral lines, though you'll also see polyethylene (black flexible pipe) in some installations, especially in areas with shifting soils. PVC is durable and handles Denver's water pressure well, but it can crack during freeze events if the system isn't properly winterized. Copper is occasionally used for the supply line between the house and the backflow preventer. Regardless of pipe type, proper winterization is critical to avoid costly repairs every spring.

faqs.question: What are swing joints and why are they important for sprinkler heads?
faqs.answer: A swing joint is a flexible connection between the lateral pipe and the sprinkler head, made from a series of threaded fittings and a short piece of funny pipe (flexible riser). They absorb impact so that when someone steps on a head or a mower clips it, the head flexes instead of cracking the pipe below. In Denver's clay soils, swing joints also make it much easier to adjust head height as the ground shifts and settles over time. Any quality installation or repair should include swing joints on every head.

faqs.question: What kind of wire connects my sprinkler controller to the valves?
faqs.answer: Sprinkler systems use direct-burial irrigation wire, typically 18-gauge multi-strand cable with a common wire plus one wire per valve zone. The common wire is usually white, and the individual zone wires are different colors to help with troubleshooting. Wire connections underground are made with waterproof connectors (often called grease caps or silicone-filled wire nuts) to prevent corrosion. Bad wire connections are one of the most frustrating problems to diagnose because a zone can work intermittently before failing completely.

faqs.question: Do I need a rain sensor on my sprinkler system in Denver?
faqs.answer: A rain sensor is a smart investment for any Denver irrigation system because it automatically shuts off your sprinklers when it's raining, preventing wasted water and potential overwatering. They're inexpensive, easy to install, and some Denver-area water districts offer rebates for them. The sensor mounts in an exposed area and uses either hygroscopic discs or electronic sensors to detect rainfall. If you have a smart controller, rain sensing is usually built in through weather data, so a separate sensor may not be necessary.

faqs.question: What is a flow sensor and does my irrigation system need one?
faqs.answer: A flow sensor monitors how much water moves through your irrigation mainline and can detect abnormal flow that indicates a broken pipe, stuck valve, or major leak. When paired with a compatible smart controller, it can automatically shut the system down if it detects a problem, saving you from a massive water bill. Flow sensors are especially valuable in Denver where a mainline break can waste thousands of gallons before anyone notices. They're a worthwhile add-on for any system, and you can learn more at 5280sprinklers.com.

faqs.question: What is a master valve and should my sprinkler system have one?
faqs.answer: A master valve sits on the mainline after the backflow preventer and only opens when the controller signals a zone to run, keeping the rest of the system depressurized between cycles. This means if a zone valve fails and gets stuck open, water won't flow continuously and run up your bill. It's basically an insurance policy against leaks and valve failures. We strongly recommend master valves for Denver properties, and most newer smart controllers have a dedicated master valve terminal built in.

faqs.question: What are the main components of a drip irrigation system?
faqs.answer: A drip system typically includes a pressure regulator, a filter, drip tubing or emitter line, individual emitters, and various fittings like barbed connectors and stakes. The pressure regulator is critical because drip operates at much lower pressure than sprinklers, and running it at full line pressure will blow the fittings apart. Drip is ideal for Denver garden beds, trees, and xeriscaped areas because it delivers water directly to the root zone with minimal evaporation. Visit 5280sprinklers.com to discuss adding drip zones to your existing system.

faqs.question: What is an MP rotator and why is it popular in Denver?
faqs.answer: An MP rotator is a multi-stream, multi-trajectory nozzle that delivers water in slow, rotating streams instead of a single fan spray. They apply water at a much lower precipitation rate than standard spray nozzles, which means less runoff on Denver's tough clay soils and sloped yards. They're also more wind-resistant than spray heads, which matters when those afternoon gusts kick up along the Front Range. MP rotators retrofit onto standard spray head bodies, so upgrading is straightforward.

faqs.question: What types of fittings are used in irrigation pipe systems?
faqs.answer: Irrigation fittings include elbows, tees, couplings, reducers, and adapters, and they come in both slip (glue) and threaded versions for PVC systems. For poly pipe systems, you'll use barbed insert fittings secured with stainless steel clamps. Using the right fitting matters because a mismatched connection is a future leak waiting to happen, especially after Denver's freeze-thaw cycles stress the joints. If you're attempting a DIY repair, make sure you match the fitting type and pipe size exactly.

faqs.question: What does a check valve do in a sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: A check valve prevents water from draining out of the lowest sprinkler heads on a zone after the valve shuts off, which is called low-head drainage. Without check valves, you'll see water pooling around the lowest heads for several minutes after each cycle, creating muddy spots and wasting water. Most modern spray bodies and rotors come with built-in check valves (sometimes labeled SAM or seal-a-matic). If your heads are flooding at the low points of your yard, retrofitting bodies with built-in check valves is a quick fix.

faqs.question: How do sprinkler rotors differ from spray heads?
faqs.answer: Spray heads pop up and emit a fixed fan of water covering a radius of about 5 to 18 feet, while rotors shoot a single or multiple streams that rotate to cover 20 to 50 feet or more. Because rotors apply water more slowly over a larger area, they need to run longer than spray heads to deliver the same amount of water, which is why you should never mix them on the same zone. Rotors are the go-to choice for large turf areas in Denver, while spray heads handle the smaller, tighter spaces.

faqs.question: What is funny pipe and where is it used in irrigation?
faqs.answer: Funny pipe is the flexible, ribbed tubing (usually blue or black) that connects the rigid lateral pipe to individual sprinkler heads through a swing joint assembly. It lets you position sprinkler heads precisely without having to make exact cuts in the mainline pipe. The flexibility also absorbs ground movement from Denver's expansive clay soils, reducing the chance of cracked fittings. It's typically sold in rolls and cut to length, with standard half-inch barbed fittings on each end.

faqs.question: Can I add a drip zone to my existing sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Absolutely, and it's one of the most common upgrades we do in Denver. You can convert an existing spray zone to drip or add a new drip zone by running a dedicated valve and line to the area you want to irrigate. The key components you'll need are a pressure regulator to drop the pressure down to around 25-30 PSI, a filter to keep emitters from clogging, and the appropriate drip tubing or emitter line for your plants. Head over to 5280sprinklers.com to schedule a drip zone addition.

faqs.question: What's the difference between PVC and poly pipe for irrigation?
faqs.answer: PVC is a rigid white pipe joined with primer and cement that handles high pressure well and is the standard for most Denver residential systems. Poly pipe is a flexible black tubing that uses barbed fittings with clamps, making it easier to install around curves and in rocky soil conditions. PVC is generally more durable long-term but is more susceptible to freeze damage if not properly winterized, while poly has some give that can handle minor ground movement. Most Denver systems use PVC for mainlines and laterals, though poly shows up in older installations and specific situations.

faqs.question: How does a sprinkler solenoid valve actually work?
faqs.answer: When your controller sends a 24-volt signal through the wire, an electromagnetic solenoid lifts a plunger inside the valve, which releases water pressure from a small chamber above the diaphragm. Once that pressure drops, the incoming water pressure pushes the diaphragm open and water flows to the sprinkler heads on that zone. When the signal stops, the solenoid closes, the chamber refills, and the diaphragm seals shut. It's a simple and reliable design, but dirt, debris, or a torn diaphragm can cause the valve to stick open or not open at all.

faqs.question: What should I look for when choosing a sprinkler controller for my Denver home?
faqs.answer: Start with the number of zones your system has and make sure the controller supports at least that many, plus a couple of extras for future expansion. For Denver, we recommend a WaterSense-labeled smart controller that adjusts to local weather conditions because our climate is so variable. Also look for features like Wi-Fi connectivity for phone-based control, a master valve terminal, and a sensor input for rain or flow sensors. faqs.question: Why do underground wire connections fail in sprinkler systems?
faqs.answer: Underground wire splices fail when moisture gets into the connection and causes corrosion, which increases resistance and eventually breaks the circuit to the valve. This happens most often when standard wire nuts are used instead of waterproof, grease-filled connectors that seal out moisture and soil chemicals. In Denver, our freeze-thaw cycles and clay soil movement put extra stress on wire connections over time, pulling splices apart or cracking old connectors. If you have a zone that works sometimes but not others, a corroded wire connection is one of the first things to check.

faqs.question: How do you decide where to place zones when designing a sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Zone design comes down to grouping areas with similar water needs — sunny front yard turf goes on a different zone than shaded perennial beds, for example. We also factor in your water pressure and flow rate so each zone runs efficiently without weak spots or misting. Slopes, soil type, and plant material all play a role in Denver's semi-arid climate. The goal is even coverage with zero waste.

faqs.answer: For garden beds, trees, and xeriscaped areas it's almost always worth it — drip delivers water directly to the root zone with far less evaporation, which matters a lot in Denver's dry air. You'll typically use 30 to 50 percent less water on those zones compared to spray heads. We can convert individual zones without touching the rest of your system. We can often retrofit those components without ripping everything out, which saves you a ton of time and money. If the pipe is polyethylene that's gone brittle or the layout no longer matches your landscaping, a full replacement makes more sense. faqs.question: What's the difference between trenching and pulling pipe for sprinkler installation?
faqs.answer: Trenching uses a machine to cut an open ditch, lay the pipe, and backfill — it's the go-to method when we need precise depth control or the soil is rocky, which is common along the Front Range. Pipe pulling uses a vibratory plow that feeds pipe underground without opening a trench, so it's faster and leaves less mess in established lawns. We choose the method based on your soil conditions, yard layout, and how much existing landscaping we need to protect.

faqs.question: What type of pipe works best for sprinkler systems in Denver's soil and climate?
faqs.answer: We use Schedule 40 PVC for mainlines and Class 200 PVC for laterals on most Denver installs — it handles our freeze-thaw cycles well as long as the system is properly winterized. Funny pipe or flexible swing joints connect the heads so they can absorb ground movement from our expansive clay soils without cracking. Some older systems used poly pipe, which was fine for its era but PVC gives better flow and longevity for new work.

faqs.question: What are the requirements for backflow preventer installation in Denver?
faqs.answer: Denver Water and most surrounding districts require a testable backflow prevention device — typically a pressure vacuum breaker or reduced pressure zone assembly — on every irrigation system tied to the municipal water supply. It has to be installed above grade, upstream of all irrigation valves, and tested annually by a certified technician. We install code-compliant backflow preventers and can handle the annual testing too. Check https://5280sprinklers.com/ to schedule your installation or test.

faqs.question: How do you design a sprinkler system for a sloped yard?
faqs.answer: Slopes need special attention because water runs off before it soaks in, and low-head drainage can drain pipes through the lowest heads after the zone shuts off. We use check valves in the heads, pressure regulation to keep everything even from top to bottom, and shorter run times with multiple cycles to prevent runoff. Drip irrigation is also a great option for steep Denver hillsides where spray heads would just waste water downhill.

faqs.question: How many sprinkler heads can I put on one zone?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on your available flow rate (GPM) and water pressure — every head uses a specific amount of water, and you can only run as many as your supply can feed without losing performance. A typical Denver residential tap might support six to eight rotor heads or ten to twelve spray heads per zone, but we measure your actual flow before designing anything. Overloading a zone leads to poor coverage, misting, and dry spots.

faqs.question: What is GPM capacity planning and why does it matter for my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: GPM stands for gallons per minute, and it's the single most important number in irrigation design — it tells us how much water your supply can deliver at any given time. If we design zones that demand more GPM than your system can provide, you'll get weak streams, poor coverage, and wasted water. We measure your static pressure and flow rate on-site before designing a single zone so everything runs at peak efficiency.

faqs.question: Can you upgrade my manual sprinkler system to an automatic one?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's one of the best quality-of-life upgrades you can make. We replace your manual valves with electric solenoid valves, run control wire back to a new controller, and program your watering schedule. You go from turning valves by hand every day to a fully automated system that runs on its own — even when you're on vacation. Get started at https://5280sprinklers.com/ to schedule the upgrade.

faqs.question: How deep do sprinkler wires need to be buried, and how is wire routed?
faqs.answer: In the Denver area we typically bury irrigation control wire six to eight inches deep — deep enough to avoid damage from aeration and light digging, but accessible if we ever need to troubleshoot. Wire runs alongside the mainline pipe in the same trench whenever possible, which keeps the install clean and minimizes yard disruption. We use direct-burial rated, multi-strand wire and waterproof connectors at every splice point to prevent corrosion from Colorado's clay moisture.

faqs.question: How do you expand sprinkler coverage to a new area of my yard?
faqs.answer: First we check whether your existing system has enough water capacity and open controller stations to support the new area. If it does, we tap into the nearest mainline, run new pipe and wire, and install heads matched to the new space. If your system is maxed out, we may need to add a dedicated zone with its own valve. Either way, the goal is seamless integration — schedule an appointment at https://5280sprinklers.com/ and we'll map out the best approach.

faqs.question: How do I know if I should replace my entire sprinkler system or just upgrade parts of it?
faqs.answer: If you're dealing with one or two problem zones, outdated heads, or an old controller, targeted upgrades are usually the smarter move — you get modern performance without tearing up your whole yard. But if you're seeing constant leaks across multiple zones, your pipe is deteriorating, or your layout no longer matches your landscaping at all, a full replacement will save you more money long-term than patching an aging system. We'll walk your property and give you an honest recommendation — schedule an evaluation at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What are WiFi sprinkler controllers and how do they work?
faqs.answer: WiFi sprinkler controllers connect to your home wireless network and let you manage your entire irrigation system from a smartphone app, no matter where you are. They pull local Denver weather data to automatically adjust watering schedules, so your lawn gets exactly what it needs without you lifting a finger. Most models replace your existing controller and wire right into your current valve setup, making the upgrade pretty straightforward.

faqs.question: Can I control my sprinkler system with Alexa or Google Home?
faqs.answer: Yes, most modern smart controllers like Rachio and Hunter Hydrawise integrate directly with Alexa and Google Home. You can use voice commands to start or stop watering, skip a scheduled run, or check system status. It is a nice convenience feature, especially when you are in the middle of a backyard barbecue and realize the sprinklers are about to kick on.

faqs.question: What is weather-based watering and why does it matter in Denver?
faqs.answer: Weather-based watering uses real-time local weather data like temperature, humidity, wind, and rainfall to automatically adjust your irrigation schedule. In Denver, where we can get a surprise afternoon thunderstorm one day and bone-dry 90-degree heat the next, this is a game changer. Your system skips watering when it rains and increases run times during heat waves, saving water and keeping your lawn healthy without constant manual adjustments.

faqs.question: What is an ET controller and do I need one?
faqs.answer: An ET (evapotranspiration) controller calculates exactly how much water your landscape loses each day based on weather conditions and adjusts irrigation run times to replace only what was lost. For Denver's semi-arid climate, ET-based controllers are one of the most effective tools for water conservation. If you are serious about keeping a healthy lawn while minimizing water waste, an ET controller is absolutely worth considering.

faqs.question: Can I control my sprinkler system remotely when I'm traveling?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. With a WiFi or cellular-connected smart controller, you can monitor and adjust your sprinkler system from anywhere with an internet connection. Heading out of town for a week? You can check that everything is running, adjust schedules if a heat wave hits Denver, or shut the whole system down if a neighbor texts you about a leak. It gives you complete peace of mind when you are away from home.

faqs.question: How does flow monitoring and leak detection work on smart sprinkler systems?
faqs.answer: Flow monitoring uses a sensor installed on your main irrigation line that measures water flow in real time. If the system detects abnormally high flow (a broken pipe or stuck valve) or flow when nothing should be running, it sends an alert to your phone and can automatically shut down the system. In Denver, where a single mainline break can waste hundreds of gallons in minutes, this feature can save you from a massive water bill and landscape damage.

faqs.question: Which smart controller is best: Rachio, Hunter Hydrawise, or Rain Bird ESP-ME3?
faqs.answer: Each has its strengths and the best choice depends on your setup. Rachio is the most user-friendly with excellent weather intelligence and a polished app. Hunter Hydrawise offers strong flow monitoring integration and is great for larger properties. Rain Bird ESP-ME3 is a modular commercial-grade controller that works well for big systems with lots of zones. We can help you pick the right one based on your property size, number of zones, and what features matter most to you.

faqs.question: How hard is it to upgrade from an old timer to a smart controller?
faqs.answer: For most Denver homes, the upgrade is surprisingly simple. Smart controllers use the same low-voltage wiring as your old timer, so it is usually a matter of removing the old unit, mounting the new one, and connecting the existing wires. The whole process typically takes about an hour. If your old wiring is damaged or you have a very old system with unusual configurations, it might take a bit longer, but we handle that regularly.

faqs.question: Are soil moisture sensors worth adding to my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Soil moisture sensors measure the actual moisture level in your root zone and prevent irrigation when the soil is already wet enough. In Denver's clay-heavy soils, which hold water differently than sandy soils, this is especially useful because it prevents overwatering that leads to runoff and root rot. They pair well with smart controllers and can significantly reduce your water usage by only watering when your landscape actually needs it.

faqs.question: What are the main benefits of upgrading to a smart sprinkler controller?
faqs.answer: Smart controllers deliver three big wins: water savings, convenience, and lawn health. They automatically adjust to Denver's unpredictable weather so you are not watering during rainstorms or underwatering during heat waves. You get full control from your phone, real-time alerts if something goes wrong, and detailed usage reports. Most homeowners see a noticeable drop in their water bill within the first season.

faqs.question: Should I get a cellular or WiFi connected sprinkler controller?
faqs.answer: WiFi controllers are the most common choice for residential properties since they use your existing home network and have no ongoing connectivity fees. Cellular controllers are ideal for properties where WiFi does not reach the controller location, like large estates, commercial sites, or detached buildings. Cellular units do typically require a small monthly data plan, but they are rock-solid reliable and do not depend on your home internet staying up.

faqs.question: How do I program a smart sprinkler controller for Denver's watering restrictions?
faqs.answer: Most smart controllers have built-in support for local watering restrictions. You set your address, and they automatically apply Denver Water's rules, including designated watering days and the no-watering window between 10 AM and 6 PM. From there, the controller handles the rest by scheduling your zones within the allowed windows and adjusting run times based on weather. If you need help with initial setup, we are happy to configure it during installation.

faqs.question: How much water can a smart controller actually save?
faqs.answer: Studies consistently show that weather-based smart controllers save between 20% and 50% on outdoor water use compared to traditional timers. In Denver, where outdoor irrigation can account for more than half of your summer water bill, those savings add up fast. The EPA's WaterSense program estimates that a typical home can save nearly 8,800 gallons per year by switching to a WaterSense-certified smart controller.

faqs.question: Will a smart controller work with my existing sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: In almost every case, yes. Smart controllers are designed as drop-in replacements for standard irrigation timers. If your current system uses standard 24-volt AC valves, which covers the vast majority of residential systems in Denver, a smart controller will work with your existing wiring and valves. We will verify compatibility during installation and let you know if anything needs to be updated.

faqs.question: Can smart irrigation technology help me comply with Colorado water regulations?
faqs.answer: Smart controllers make compliance with Colorado water regulations nearly effortless. They automatically enforce watering day restrictions, time-of-day windows, and can respond to drought mandates by reducing usage across all zones. Some municipalities even offer rebates for installing WaterSense-certified smart controllers. With the ongoing focus on water conservation along the Front Range, upgrading to smart technology puts you ahead of future regulations too.

faqs.question: What kind of return on investment can I expect from upgrading my irrigation system?
faqs.answer: A well-designed irrigation system protects your landscaping investment, reduces water waste, and can increase your property value. Most Denver homeowners see measurable water bill reductions within the first season after upgrading to efficient heads and a smart controller. Over a few years, the water savings alone can offset a significant portion of the upgrade cost, and a green, healthy lawn boosts curb appeal if you ever decide to sell.

faqs.question: What happens if I skip regular sprinkler maintenance?
faqs.answer: Skipping maintenance is a false economy. Small issues like a leaking valve or a tilted head that sprays onto the sidewalk get worse over time, wasting water and stressing your lawn. Eventually, those ignored problems turn into bigger repairs like dead zones in your yard, flooded areas, or a full mainline break. Investing in seasonal maintenance is always cheaper than dealing with the cascade of problems that come from neglect.

faqs.question: How much can a sprinkler system impact my monthly water bill?
faqs.answer: An inefficient or broken sprinkler system can easily double or triple your summer water bill in Denver. Common culprits include heads spraying onto concrete, zones running too long, leaking valves, and outdated controllers that ignore weather. A properly maintained and well-programmed system keeps your water usage in check and can make a dramatic difference in what Denver Water charges you each month during irrigation season.

faqs.answer: A good rule of thumb for Denver homeowners is to plan for three key service touchpoints each year: spring startup, a mid-season checkup, and fall winterization. Budgeting for all three keeps your system running efficiently and catches small problems before they become expensive repairs. faqs.question: Is it cheaper to do sprinkler repairs myself or hire a professional?
faqs.answer: Simple tasks like replacing a broken pop-up head are reasonable DIY jobs if you are handy. But for anything involving valves, wiring, mainline repairs, or backflow testing, hiring a pro usually saves money in the long run. Misdiagnosed problems and improper repairs can cause more damage, waste water, and end up costing significantly more than getting it done right the first time. faqs.question: When does it make more sense to replace my sprinkler system than keep repairing it?
faqs.answer: If you are calling for repairs multiple times per season, your system is more than 15-20 years old, or you are dealing with outdated pipe materials and constant leaks, replacement often makes more financial sense. The tipping point is when annual repair costs start approaching what you would pay for a new, efficient system that will run trouble-free for years.
