faqs.question: How much damage can a sprinkler leak cause if left unrepaired?
faqs.answer: An undetected sprinkler leak can cause serious damage beyond just wasting water. We have seen leaks erode foundations, flood window wells, kill sections of lawn from oversaturation, and create breeding grounds for mosquitoes. In Denver's expansive clay soils, excess water near your foundation can cause heaving and structural movement. A small leak that costs little to fix today can turn into thousands in water damage and landscaping repairs if ignored.

faqs.question: Is preventive sprinkler maintenance really worth the cost?
faqs.answer: Preventive maintenance is one of the best investments you can make in your irrigation system. A seasonal checkup catches worn nozzles, misaligned heads, slow leaks, and programming errors before they waste water or damage your landscape. The cost of a maintenance visit is a fraction of what you would pay for an emergency repair or the water waste from a system running inefficiently all summer. Think of it like an oil change for your lawn.

faqs.question: What sprinkler repairs are safe to do myself?
faqs.answer: Most homeowners can safely handle simple tasks like replacing a broken sprinkler head, adjusting spray patterns, or cleaning clogged nozzles. These are low-risk fixes that don't involve cutting into mainlines or working with electrical components. If you're comfortable turning a wrench and following a YouTube tutorial, you can knock these out in under an hour.

faqs.question: When should I call a professional instead of fixing my sprinkler system myself?
faqs.answer: Call a pro when you're dealing with mainline breaks, backflow preventer issues, valve wiring problems, or anything involving your water meter connection. If water is pooling in your yard and you can't identify the source, that's another sign to get expert eyes on it. Here in Denver, any work involving backflow testing legally requires a certified technician. Visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ to get on our schedule.

faqs.question: What tools do I need for basic sprinkler repairs?
faqs.answer: A solid starter kit includes a flat-head screwdriver, a sprinkler head adjustment tool (often included with new heads), needle-nose pliers, Teflon tape, and a small shovel or trowel for digging around heads. A spare set of matched nozzles from your local Denver hardware store is also smart to keep on hand. You don't need anything fancy — most basic repairs use tools you probably already own.

faqs.question: Can I winterize my sprinkler system myself, or is that too risky?
faqs.answer: DIY winterization is one of the riskiest things you can attempt with your irrigation system in Denver. You need a commercial-grade air compressor that delivers the right CFM at controlled PSI — too much pressure shatters PVC pipes and fittings underground, and too little leaves water in the lines that freezes and cracks them during our Colorado winters. A botched blowout can easily cause hundreds or thousands of dollars in spring repair bills. This is the one service we strongly recommend leaving to a professional — book at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How do I replace a broken sprinkler head myself?
faqs.answer: First, turn off the water to your system. Dig carefully around the broken head to expose the riser, then unscrew the old head counterclockwise. Wrap Teflon tape on the threads of the new head, screw it on hand-tight plus a quarter turn, and backfill the soil so the head sits flush with the ground. Run the zone to check for leaks and adjust the spray pattern — the whole job takes about 15 minutes once you get the hang of it.

faqs.question: What are the most common DIY sprinkler repair mistakes?
faqs.answer: The biggest ones we see in Denver are using the wrong head type for the zone (rotors where sprays should be, or vice versa), overtightening fittings until they crack, burying heads too deep or leaving them too high, and forgetting Teflon tape on threaded connections. Another classic mistake is not matching nozzle precipitation rates within a zone, which creates dry spots and soggy patches. Taking a photo of your setup before you start any work can save you a lot of headaches.

faqs.question: Are there safety concerns I should know about before working on my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Yes — a few important ones. Your irrigation system runs on 24V AC power at the valves, which is low voltage but can still give you a jolt if you're working with wet hands on exposed wiring. Water pressure in Denver municipal systems typically runs 50-80 PSI, and an uncapped line can spray unexpectedly. Always shut off the water supply and turn off the controller before doing any work, and know where your main shutoff is before you start digging.

faqs.question: When does DIY sprinkler repair end up costing more than hiring a pro?
faqs.answer: It happens more often than you'd think. If you buy the wrong parts, crack a fitting by overtightening, or accidentally break a lateral line while digging, a simple head swap can turn into a $300+ repair. We also see homeowners rent air compressors for DIY winterization, damage their system, then pay for both the rental and professional repairs in the spring. If you're unsure about a fix, getting a quote first often saves money in the long run — schedule an appointment at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How do I clean a sprinkler valve myself?
faqs.answer: Turn off the water and release pressure by briefly running the zone. Remove the solenoid (the cylinder on top of the valve) and unscrew the valve bonnet to access the diaphragm. Rinse the diaphragm and valve body with clean water, checking for small rocks, dirt, or debris that prevent the valve from sealing. Reassemble in reverse order, making sure the diaphragm seats evenly — a crooked diaphragm is the number one reason valves leak after cleaning.

faqs.question: What should I understand about my sprinkler system before attempting any DIY work?
faqs.answer: Know how many zones you have, where your valve boxes are located, what type of heads are on each zone (rotors, sprays, or drip), and where your backflow preventer and main shutoff are. Walk your property with the controller running each zone so you can see what's connected to what. Understanding your system layout before you start digging prevents accidentally cutting into a pressurized line or working on the wrong zone.

faqs.question: How do I explain my sprinkler problem to a technician so they can help quickly?
faqs.answer: The most helpful info you can give us is: which zone number is affected, what you're seeing (low pressure, no water, constant running, leak), and roughly where in your yard it's happening. If you can snap a photo or a short video of the issue while the system is running, that's even better. Knowing whether the problem started suddenly or got worse over time helps our techs show up with the right parts on the truck.

faqs.question: How should I prepare for a sprinkler service call?
faqs.answer: Make sure we can access your backflow preventer, controller, and valve boxes — clear away any patio furniture, garden hoses, or debris. If you have a gate, either leave it unlocked or let us know the code when you book. It helps to have your controller powered on and your water supply turned on before we arrive. You can book and add notes about access at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What happens during a spring sprinkler startup service?
faqs.answer: We slowly pressurize your system to avoid shocking pipes that have been dry all winter, then walk every zone checking for broken heads, leaks, misaligned spray patterns, and valve function. We also inspect your backflow preventer, test your controller programming, and adjust run times for Denver's early-season watering needs. You'll get a summary of anything we found and our recommendations before we leave.

faqs.question: What exactly happens during sprinkler winterization?
faqs.answer: We connect a commercial air compressor to your system through the blowout port and systematically push compressed air through each zone, forcing all remaining water out of the pipes, heads, and valves. We control the PSI carefully to avoid damaging components — too much pressure is just as bad as leaving water in the lines. Once every zone is clear, we shut down the controller and turn off the water supply so your system is fully protected against Denver's freeze-thaw cycles.

faqs.question: What should I expect during a sprinkler repair visit?
faqs.answer: Our tech will start by talking with you about the issue, then run the affected zones to diagnose the problem firsthand. Most common repairs — broken heads, leaking valves, wiring issues — can be fixed on the spot in a single visit. If we find something that requires a follow-up (like a mainline break that needs excavation), we'll explain the scope and schedule the work at a time that works for you.

faqs.question: How does leak detection work for sprinkler systems?
faqs.answer: We use a combination of visual inspection, pressure testing, and zone-by-zone isolation to pinpoint where water is escaping. Sometimes a leak is obvious — a geyser in your front yard — but often it's a slow underground seep that shows up as a mushy spot or an unusually high water bill. Our techs know the common failure points for Denver soils and installation styles, which speeds up the process significantly.

faqs.question: How long does each type of sprinkler service take?
faqs.answer: A spring startup typically takes 30-60 minutes depending on the number of zones. Winterization blowouts run about 20-45 minutes. Standard repairs average 30-90 minutes, though complex issues like mainline breaks can take longer. Leak detection varies the most — a straightforward leak might take 30 minutes to find, while a hidden one could take a couple of hours to isolate.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my yard before a sprinkler service?
faqs.answer: Clear access to your backflow preventer (usually on the side of the house), your controller, and any valve boxes in the yard. Trim back plants or grass that may be covering sprinkler heads or valve box lids — our techs need to see and reach everything. If you have pets, we appreciate a heads-up so we can coordinate with you on keeping gates closed.

faqs.question: What does 5280 Sprinklers check during a system inspection?
faqs.answer: We run every zone and check head coverage, spray patterns, and rotation on rotors. We inspect valves for leaks and proper operation, test the backflow preventer, review your controller programming, and look for signs of pipe damage or settling. We also check water pressure at the source, because Denver water pressure can vary by neighborhood and elevation, and high pressure is a leading cause of blown fittings.

faqs.question: What is an irrigation system audit and do I need one?
faqs.answer: An irrigation audit is a deep-dive evaluation of your entire system's performance — we measure head-to-head coverage, check precipitation rates, identify pressure issues, and look for design flaws that waste water. It's especially valuable if you've noticed uneven growth, high water bills, or if your system is more than 10 years old. Denver Water occasionally offers rebates tied to audit-driven improvements, so it can pay for itself.

faqs.question: What does a water efficiency assessment involve for my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: We analyze your system's water usage against the actual needs of your landscape, factoring in Denver's semi-arid climate, your soil type, sun exposure, and plant material. We identify zones that are overwatering or underwatering and recommend adjustments like nozzle changes, schedule tweaks, or adding rain sensors and smart controllers. Many Denver homeowners cut their outdoor water use by 20-30% after an efficiency assessment without sacrificing lawn health.

faqs.question: Can lawn care services work alongside my irrigation schedule?
faqs.answer: Absolutely — in fact, coordinating lawn care and irrigation is one of the best things you can do for your yard in Denver's climate. Aeration and fertilization interact with how much and when you water, so having both services in sync prevents overwatering after aeration or washing away fresh fertilizer. Let us know who handles your lawn care and we can adjust your irrigation schedule to complement their timing. Schedule an appointment at https://5280sprinklers.com/ to discuss your setup.

faqs.question: How do Rain Bird, Hunter, and Toro sprinkler systems compare for Denver homes?
faqs.answer: All three are solid brands, but each has strengths. Rain Bird is the most widely installed in the Denver metro and has excellent parts availability. Hunter offers some of the best smart controller technology on the market. Toro tends to be more budget-friendly while still holding up well in our climate. We work with all three and can recommend the best fit based on your yard size, budget, and water goals.

faqs.question: What sprinkler brand works best for Denver's climate?
faqs.answer: Rain Bird and Hunter are the two brands we install and service most often in the Denver area, and both handle our altitude, dry summers, and freeze-thaw cycles really well. Rain Bird has a slight edge in parts availability locally, while Hunter's smart controllers are great for water conservation in our semi-arid climate. Ultimately, proper installation and seasonal maintenance matter more than the brand name on the box.

faqs.question: Is the Rain Bird ESP-TM2 controller a good choice for Denver yards?
faqs.answer: The Rain Bird ESP-TM2 is one of the most popular controllers we install in Denver. It supports up to 12 zones out of the box and is expandable, so it handles everything from small front yards to larger properties. It's also Wi-Fi ready with the LNK2 module, which lets you adjust schedules from your phone — really handy when Denver's weather flips from 90 degrees to a surprise hailstorm. It's reliable, reasonably priced, and easy for homeowners to use.

faqs.question: What are the advantages of the Hunter Pro-HC controller?
faqs.answer: The Hunter Pro-HC is a strong smart controller option that connects to Wi-Fi and integrates with Hunter's Hydrawise platform. It automatically adjusts watering based on local weather data, which is a big deal in Denver where conditions change fast. The app is intuitive and lets you manage everything remotely, including seasonal adjustments and rain delays. We recommend it for homeowners who want set-it-and-forget-it water savings without sacrificing lawn health.

faqs.question: Why do so many Denver irrigation pros recommend MP Rotator nozzles?
faqs.answer: MP Rotator nozzles deliver water in slow, multi-trajectory streams instead of a single spray, which means much less runoff and wind drift — both common problems along the Front Range. They apply water at a matched precipitation rate regardless of the arc or radius, so you get even coverage without dry spots. They also use about 30% less water than traditional spray nozzles, which helps keep your bill in check during Denver's mandatory watering restrictions.

faqs.question: Are Rain Bird 1800 series spray heads reliable in Colorado?
faqs.answer: The Rain Bird 1800 series is basically the industry workhorse — we install and replace more of these than any other pop-up spray head in the Denver metro. They come in 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12-inch pop-up heights, so they work for everything from ground cover to tall ornamental grasses. The built-in check valve on SAM models prevents low-head drainage, which is important on Denver's sloped lots. They're durable, affordable, and compatible with a wide range of nozzles.

faqs.question: How long do Hunter PGP rotors last in Denver's conditions?
faqs.answer: Hunter PGP rotors are some of the most durable gear-driven rotors on the market, and in Denver we typically see them last 8 to 15 years with proper maintenance. The main things that shorten their life here are freeze damage from improper winterization and sediment from our hard water clogging the filter screen. We recommend pulling and inspecting PGP rotors during your spring startup to clean the screens and check for any freeze-related cracking.

faqs.question: Can I mix Rain Bird and Hunter products on the same irrigation system?
faqs.answer: You can mix brands in different zones without any issues — for example, a Rain Bird controller running Hunter rotors on one zone and Rain Bird spray heads on another works just fine. What you want to avoid is mixing different head types or brands within the same zone, because different precipitation rates will give you uneven coverage with wet and dry spots. If you're replacing heads on an existing zone, match the brand and model that's already there for best results.

faqs.question: Where can I buy replacement sprinkler parts in Denver?
faqs.answer: For basic parts like nozzles and spray heads, most Denver-area Home Depot and Lowe's locations carry Rain Bird and Hunter products. For professional-grade parts and harder-to-find items, check out SiteOne Landscape Supply or Horizon Distributors — both have multiple locations along the Front Range. If you'd rather not hunt down parts yourself, visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ to book a repair and we'll bring everything we need.

faqs.question: What do manufacturer warranties cover on sprinkler products?
faqs.answer: Rain Bird typically offers a 5-year warranty on controllers and a 3- to 5-year warranty on heads and valves. Hunter provides a 5-year residential warranty on most products and 2 years on commercial. Toro generally offers 3 to 5 years depending on the product line. Keep in mind that manufacturer warranties cover defects, not damage from freezing, improper installation, or normal wear — that's where proper winterization and spring startups really pay off.

faqs.answer: This comes up a lot, especially with systems that are 15+ years old. The good news is that both Rain Bird and Hunter design newer products to be backward-compatible with common fittings and pipe sizes. In most cases, we can swap in a current-generation head or valve without re-plumbing anything. If your controller is the discontinued piece, upgrading to a modern smart controller is usually a straightforward swap that also saves water. faqs.question: Which sprinkler brand holds up best through Denver's freeze-thaw cycles?
faqs.answer: Both Rain Bird and Hunter make products that handle Denver's freeze-thaw cycles well, but the real difference-maker is proper winterization — not the brand. That said, heads with built-in check valves (like the Rain Bird 1800 SAM series) resist freeze damage better because they prevent water from pooling in low-point lines. Brass and stainless steel components also outlast plastic in extreme temperature swings. The single best thing you can do for any brand is get a professional blowout before the first hard freeze each fall.

faqs.question: How should I adjust my sprinkler schedule after fertilizing my Denver lawn?
faqs.answer: After applying fertilizer, water your lawn lightly — about 15 to 20 minutes per zone — to wash the granules off the grass blades and into the soil. This prevents fertilizer burn, which is especially common during Denver's hot, dry summers. For the next few days, keep to your normal watering schedule but make sure you're hitting each zone consistently. Avoid heavy watering right after application, as it can wash the fertilizer past the root zone before it does any good.

faqs.question: Should I change my irrigation schedule around lawn aeration?
faqs.answer: Yes — water your lawn thoroughly the day before aeration so the soil is moist enough for the aerator to pull clean plugs. Denver's clay-heavy soil is brutal to aerate when it's dry. After aeration, resume your normal watering schedule right away to help the soil recover and the holes stay open for air, water, and nutrients to reach the roots. This is one of the best things you can do for a Denver lawn, especially in September when the soil has been compacted all summer.

faqs.question: What's the right watering schedule when overseeding my lawn in Denver?
faqs.answer: When overseeding, the goal is to keep the top half-inch of soil consistently moist until the new seed germinates — usually 10 to 21 days for bluegrass, less for ryegrass. In Denver's dry air, that typically means running short cycles 2 to 3 times per day rather than one long soak. Once the new grass is about 2 inches tall, start transitioning back to deeper, less frequent watering. Early September is the ideal overseeding window here because the soil is still warm but the daytime heat is tapering off.

faqs.question: How much should I water new sod in Denver?
faqs.answer: New sod needs a lot of water in Denver's dry climate — plan on watering 3 to 4 times daily for the first two weeks to keep the soil beneath the sod consistently moist. After about two weeks, reduce to twice daily, then once daily by week three or four as the roots establish. By week six, you should be transitioning to a normal deep-watering schedule of 2 to 3 times per week. If you need help programming your controller for a sod schedule, visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ and we can set it up for you.

faqs.question: How long should I wait to water after applying weed killer?
faqs.answer: It depends on the product type. For post-emergent liquid herbicides (the kind you spray on existing weeds), wait at least 24 hours before watering so the product has time to absorb through the leaves. For granular pre-emergent herbicides, you actually want to water within 24 to 48 hours to activate the product and wash it into the soil. Always check the product label, but those are the general rules we follow for Denver lawns. Getting this timing wrong is one of the most common reasons weed treatments fail.

faqs.question: Does mowing height affect how much I need to water my Denver lawn?
faqs.answer: Absolutely — and this is one of the most underrated water-saving tips for Denver homeowners. Keeping your bluegrass at 3 to 3.5 inches shades the soil, reduces evaporation, and encourages deeper roots that access moisture lower in the soil profile. Lawns mowed too short (under 2.5 inches) lose moisture fast in our dry air and intense sun, meaning you'll need to water significantly more to keep them from browning out. Taller grass also shades the soil more effectively, so it's a win all around.

faqs.question: Can I run my sprinklers right after applying herbicide to my lawn?
faqs.answer: For most liquid herbicide applications, no — running sprinklers too soon will wash the product off the weed leaves before it can be absorbed, wasting your time and money. Wait at least 24 hours, and ideally 48 hours if rain isn't in the forecast. If you applied a granular product, it's the opposite — you want to water it in within a day or two to activate it. When in doubt, read the label carefully or ask your lawn care provider for specific timing based on the product they used.

faqs.question: What does a seasonal lawn care and irrigation calendar look like for Denver?
faqs.answer: Here's the quick version: In spring (late April/May), get your system started up and begin light watering as temps warm up. Summer (June-August) is peak irrigation — water deeply 2 to 3 times per week following any local restrictions. Early fall (September) is prime time for aeration, overseeding, and fertilizing while you start dialing back the watering. By late October, schedule your blowout before the first hard freeze. Winter is hands-off for irrigation, but a good time to plan any system upgrades for next season.

faqs.question: How do I prevent lawn fungus through better watering practices in Denver?
faqs.answer: The number one rule is water early in the morning — between 4 AM and 8 AM — so the grass blades dry before evening. Watering in the late afternoon or at night leaves moisture sitting on the lawn overnight, which is an open invitation for fungal diseases like necrotic ring spot and summer patch, both common along the Front Range. Also, water deeply but infrequently rather than light daily sprinkles, which keep the surface perpetually damp. If you're seeing brown patches that don't respond to more water, it might already be fungus — stop increasing your run times and get a diagnosis first.

faqs.question: When should I start watering again after core aeration?
faqs.answer: Start watering the same day or the next morning after core aeration — there's no need to wait. The aeration holes allow water to penetrate deeper into Denver's clay soil, so this is actually the best time to give your lawn a good deep soak. If you overseeded at the same time (which we highly recommend in September), switch to shorter, more frequent watering cycles to keep the seed moist. The combination of aeration plus consistent irrigation is one of the fastest ways to improve a struggling Denver lawn.

faqs.question: How should I adjust my irrigation system during a full lawn renovation?
faqs.answer: A full lawn renovation — whether you're killing off the old lawn and starting from seed or laying new sod — requires a completely different irrigation approach than an established lawn. You'll need to reprogram your controller for multiple short cycles throughout the day to keep the soil surface moist during establishment. Plan on 3 to 4 daily cycles for the first two to three weeks, then gradually reduce frequency as roots take hold. Visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ to schedule a consultation — we can program your controller for a phased renovation schedule and make sure your system has the coverage to handle it.

faqs.question: Does the overall health of my lawn affect how much irrigation it needs?
faqs.answer: A healthy, well-established lawn with deep roots actually needs less water than a stressed or thin lawn. Dense turf shades the soil and reduces evaporation, while deep root systems can pull moisture from further down in the soil profile. On the flip side, a thin or compacted lawn loses water to evaporation and runoff much faster, so you end up using more water for worse results. Investing in aeration, proper fertilization, and correct mowing height can actually lower your water bill over time — it's one of those cases where spending a little on lawn care saves a lot on water.

faqs.question: What are Denver Water's current watering restrictions?
faqs.answer: Denver Water enforces a summer watering schedule that typically limits lawn irrigation to certain days based on your address. Watering is only allowed between 6 PM and 10 AM, and you can't water during rain or high winds. Rules change year to year, so check Denver Water's site or visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ and we'll make sure your controller is programmed to stay compliant.

faqs.question: Does Aurora have different watering rules than Denver?
faqs.answer: Yes, Aurora Water has its own set of restrictions that differ from Denver Water's rules. Aurora typically assigns watering days based on your street address and enforces stricter limits during drought years, including possible total outdoor watering bans. If you're in Aurora, we can set your irrigation controller to match their specific schedule so you avoid fines. Visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ for help getting your system dialed in.

faqs.question: How does Denver's clay soil affect my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Denver's heavy clay soil absorbs water very slowly, which means runoff is a huge problem if you run your sprinklers too long in one cycle. The fix is cycle-and-soak programming, where you break each zone into shorter run times with pauses in between so water actually soaks in instead of running down the gutter. Clay also expands and contracts with moisture changes, which can shift pipes and pop heads out of alignment over time. We deal with clay soil issues every single day across the Denver metro, so schedule an appointment at https://5280sprinklers.com/ if your system needs adjusting.

faqs.question: Does Denver's altitude affect how my sprinklers perform?
faqs.answer: At 5,280 feet, Denver's thinner air and lower atmospheric pressure cause water to evaporate faster from both the soil and the spray in the air. You'll generally need to water slightly more than the manufacturer's baseline recommendations suggest, and morning watering becomes even more critical to reduce evaporation losses. Wind is also more of a factor at altitude, so head selection and spacing really matter. If your coverage seems patchy, schedule a check at https://5280sprinklers.com/ and we'll evaluate your setup.

faqs.question: When should I turn on my sprinklers in spring and shut them down in fall in Denver?
faqs.answer: Denver's last average freeze date is around May 5th, so most folks do their spring startup in late April to mid-May. For fall, the first freeze usually hits around October 7th, and you should get your system blown out before then, ideally by late September or early October. These are averages though, and Denver weather is unpredictable, so keep an eye on forecasts. Book your startup or blowout at https://5280sprinklers.com/ so you don't miss the window.

faqs.question: Do I need a permit to install a sprinkler system in Denver?
faqs.answer: In most Denver metro jurisdictions, you'll need a plumbing permit for a new irrigation system installation, primarily because of the backflow prevention device that connects to your potable water supply. The city will require an inspection of the backflow preventer to make sure your drinking water is protected. Permit requirements vary slightly between Denver, Aurora, Lakewood, and other municipalities. We handle the permitting process as part of our installations, so head to https://5280sprinklers.com/ to get started.

faqs.question: What do homeowners need to know about Colorado water rights?
faqs.answer: Colorado is a prior appropriation state, meaning water rights are allocated by seniority rather than property ownership. For most residential homeowners on municipal water, this doesn't affect your day-to-day sprinkler use because your water provider holds the rights. However, if you have a well or want to collect rainwater, there are specific Colorado laws to follow, and rain barrel collection was only legalized recently with limits. If you have questions about how this affects your irrigation setup, visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ and we can point you in the right direction.

faqs.question: Can I still have irrigation if I xeriscape my Denver yard?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Xeriscape doesn't mean zero water, it means water-wise, and even drought-tolerant plants need irrigation to get established and during Denver's driest stretches. Drip irrigation zones work perfectly for xeriscape beds, delivering water right to the root zone without waste. Many Denver homeowners combine xeriscape areas with a small turf zone and use separate irrigation schedules for each. We design hybrid systems like this all the time, so check out https://5280sprinklers.com/ to explore your options.

faqs.question: Should I water my lawn during Denver's dry winters?
faqs.answer: Yes, winter watering is critical in Denver, especially for trees, perennials, and even dormant turf during extended dry spells. Denver can go weeks without precipitation in winter, and our low humidity and chinook winds pull moisture from the soil fast. Water once or twice a month on days when temperatures are above 40 degrees and there's no snow cover. Your irrigation system will be blown out by then, so use a hose and sprinkler. If you need help planning for it, visit https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: Can hail damage my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Denver's notorious hailstorms can absolutely damage exposed sprinkler components, especially pop-up heads, rotors, and valve box covers. Large hail can crack plastic nozzles, break head casings, and even dent or bend risers. After any significant hailstorm, it's worth doing a visual inspection and running each zone to check for damage. If you spot issues, schedule a repair at https://5280sprinklers.com/ before the damage leads to bigger problems.

faqs.question: What does Denver require for backflow prevention on irrigation systems?
faqs.answer: Denver and most surrounding municipalities require a testable backflow prevention device on all irrigation systems connected to the municipal water supply. The most common type required is a reduced pressure (RP) backflow preventer, which must be tested annually by a certified tester. If your backflow device fails the test or you don't have one, you could face fines or even have your water shut off. We handle backflow installation, testing, and repairs, so visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ to stay compliant.

faqs.question: Why does my water pressure seem different from my neighbor's in Denver?
faqs.answer: Water pressure in the Denver metro varies significantly by neighborhood, elevation, and proximity to water mains and pressure zones. Homes at higher elevations like parts of Highlands Ranch or Ken Caryl often have different pressure than homes in lower areas like Park Hill or Wash Park. Pressure can also drop during peak summer watering hours when everyone's system is running. If your sprinklers aren't performing well, the first thing we check is your static pressure, so schedule an appointment at https://5280sprinklers.com/ for a system evaluation.

faqs.question: My HOA has specific irrigation requirements. Can you help with that?

Some HOAs mandate that front yards maintain green turf during summer, which means your irrigation system has to be dialed in perfectly. We work with homeowners across dozens of HOA communities and can design or adjust your system to meet their requirements. Head to https://5280sprinklers.com/ and let us know your HOA's specs.

faqs.question: What soil types are common across the Denver metro and how do they affect drainage?
faqs.answer: The Denver metro has a mix of heavy clay (most common, especially in the southern suburbs), sandy loam near river corridors like the Platte, and rocky soil in foothill communities. Clay drains very slowly and causes runoff, sandy soil drains too fast and doesn't retain moisture, and rocky soil can be tough to trench through for pipe installation. Knowing your soil type is critical for setting run times and choosing the right precipitation rate for your heads. We can assess your specific conditions, so visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ to learn more.

faqs.answer: Yes, Denver Water and several other Denver metro water providers offer rebates for water-efficient upgrades including smart irrigation controllers, high-efficiency nozzles, and xeriscape conversions. Denver Water's rebate programs change annually, but they've historically offered significant incentives for replacing turf with water-wise landscaping. faqs.question: How do I calculate GPM for proper sprinkler zone design?
faqs.answer: GPM (gallons per minute) for zone design starts with knowing your available water supply flow rate, which you can measure with a bucket test or a flow gauge on your main line. Once you know your total available GPM, you add up the GPM of every head on a zone, and that total can't exceed about 75% of your available supply to maintain good pressure. For example, if your supply delivers 12 GPM, each zone should max out around 9 GPM. If you want help getting this right, visit https://5280sprinklers.com/ for a professional design.

faqs.question: What's the relationship between PSI and GPM in an irrigation system?
faqs.answer: PSI (pressure) and GPM (flow) have an inverse relationship in your irrigation system. As you add more heads to a zone and increase the GPM demand, the pressure at each head drops. Every sprinkler head needs a minimum operating pressure to produce its rated coverage pattern and precipitation rate. If you push too much flow through undersized pipes or add too many heads, pressure drops and your coverage falls apart. We size systems to balance both, so check out https://5280sprinklers.com/ if your coverage seems uneven.

faqs.question: What are the basics of hydraulic design for a residential sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Hydraulic design is about making sure every head on every zone gets the pressure and flow it needs to work properly. You start with your static water pressure and available GPM at the source, then account for pressure losses through the meter, backflow device, valves, pipe friction, and elevation changes. Whatever pressure is left at the last head on the zone is what determines your head selection and spacing. It sounds complicated, but it's what separates a great system from a mediocre one. We handle the math at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What does 'matched precipitation rate' mean and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: Matched precipitation rate means every head on a zone puts down water at the same rate, measured in inches per hour, regardless of the arc or radius it's covering. A quarter-circle head covers less area than a full-circle head, so it needs to put out proportionally less water to match. If rates aren't matched, some areas get soaked while others stay dry, even if run times are identical. Most modern nozzle sets are designed to match automatically, but only if you install them correctly. We ensure matched precipitation on every system we touch at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How do I figure out how many heads I can put on one zone?
faqs.answer: Zone capacity is determined by your available GPM. Add up the flow rate of every head you want on the zone and make sure the total stays under 75% of your measured supply flow. Each head type has a published GPM rating at a given pressure, so look those up from the manufacturer's spec sheet. Also consider the pipe diameter feeding the zone, because undersized pipe creates friction loss that robs pressure from the heads. For a system designed right the first time, visit https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What's the difference between static and dynamic water pressure?
faqs.answer: Static pressure is the pressure in your system when no water is flowing, and it's typically the highest reading you'll see on a gauge. Dynamic pressure is the pressure while water is actually running through the system, and it's always lower than static due to friction and flow demand. The difference between the two tells you a lot about your system's capacity. If you have 65 PSI static but it drops to 30 PSI dynamic, you've got a flow restriction somewhere that needs attention. We diagnose these issues routinely at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How does friction loss in pipes affect my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Every foot of pipe and every fitting in your irrigation system creates friction that reduces water pressure. Longer pipe runs, smaller pipe diameters, and higher flow rates all increase friction loss. For example, pushing 10 GPM through 3/4-inch pipe over 100 feet loses far more pressure than the same flow through 1-inch pipe. This is why proper pipe sizing matters so much during installation. If you're experiencing weak heads at the end of a zone, friction loss is often the culprit. Let us evaluate your system at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How should sprinkler heads be spaced for proper coverage?
faqs.answer: The golden rule is head-to-head coverage, meaning each sprinkler head should throw water all the way to the next head in the pattern. If a head has a 15-foot radius, heads should be spaced no more than 15 feet apart. This overlap is intentional and necessary because sprinkler output tapers off toward the edges. Most manufacturers recommend spacing at 50-55% of the head's diameter of throw. Wider spacing creates dry spots that no amount of extra run time will fix. We design with proper spacing every time at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How do I choose the right nozzle for my sprinkler heads?
faqs.answer: Nozzle selection depends on the area you need to cover, the arc of throw, your available pressure, and what precipitation rate you need to match across the zone. Most modern spray head nozzles come in matched precipitation rate sets where you pick the radius and arc, and the flow rate is already calculated to match. For rotors, you select nozzles based on the radius needed and confirm the GPM works within your zone budget. Manufacturer nozzle charts make this straightforward once you know your numbers. We can handle nozzle selection for you at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the precipitation rate of my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: Precipitation rate is how many inches of water your system applies per hour, and the formula is: (96.25 x total GPM of the zone) divided by the area in square feet the zone covers. For example, a zone putting out 8 GPM over 1,000 square feet has a precipitation rate of about 0.77 inches per hour. Knowing this number is essential for programming accurate run times because it tells you exactly how long to run each zone to apply a specific amount of water. If math isn't your thing, we calculate this for every system we service at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What are the biggest winterization mistakes people make?
faqs.answer: The number one mistake is waiting too long and getting caught by an early freeze, which can crack pipes, valves, and backflow devices. The second biggest mistake is not using enough air volume to fully clear every zone, leaving trapped water that expands and causes damage. Some folks also make the mistake of using too much air pressure (over 80 PSI), which can melt PVC fittings or damage poly pipe. Get it done right and on time by booking your blowout at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What mistakes should I avoid during spring sprinkler startup?
faqs.answer: The biggest spring startup mistake is turning the water on too fast, which creates a water hammer that can crack pipes and blow fittings apart. You should open the main valve slowly over 30-60 seconds to let the system pressurize gradually. Another common error is not walking every zone to check for heads that were damaged over winter or knocked out of alignment. Skipping that inspection means you might water your sidewalk all summer without knowing it. Schedule a proper startup at https://5280sprinklers.com/ and we'll catch everything.

faqs.question: Is it true that watering more always means a healthier lawn?
faqs.answer: No, and this is one of the most persistent myths in lawn care. Overwatering actually damages your lawn by suffocating roots, promoting fungal disease, and encouraging shallow root growth that makes grass less drought-resistant. Most Denver lawns need about 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week during peak summer, applied in two or three deep waterings rather than daily light sprinkles. If your grass is mushy underfoot or you see mushrooms popping up, you're probably overdoing it. We can dial in your schedule at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What happens if I use the wrong type of sprinkler head for an area?
faqs.answer: Using the wrong head type is a recipe for wasted water and patchy coverage. Spray heads are designed for small areas under about 15 feet, while rotors handle larger areas from 15 to 50+ feet. Putting spray heads in a large yard means you need way more heads and zones, and mixing spray heads and rotors on the same zone is a disaster because they have very different precipitation rates. The result is some areas drowning while others stay bone dry. If your coverage looks uneven, let us evaluate your head types at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How bad is it to ignore a small leak in my sprinkler system?
faqs.answer: That small leak is costing you more than you think. Even a tiny weeping fitting or cracked head can waste hundreds of gallons per month and create saturated spots that damage your lawn, foundation, or hardscaping. Small leaks also tend to become big leaks as water pressure erodes the damaged area over time. The sooner you fix it, the cheaper the repair and the lower your water bill. Don't ignore it, just head to https://5280sprinklers.com/ and get it taken care of.

faqs.question: Do I really need to adjust my sprinkler schedule throughout the season?
faqs.answer: Yes, and not doing so is one of the most common mistakes we see. Your lawn's water needs in June are very different from August or September. Running the same schedule from May through October means you're overwatering in spring and fall while possibly underwatering in peak summer. A smart controller handles this automatically, but even a basic controller should be adjusted at least monthly. If you want to set it and forget it the right way, ask us about smart controllers at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: Why is it wasteful to run sprinklers during rain?
faqs.answer: It sounds obvious, but we see it constantly: sprinklers happily running during a rainstorm. Besides wasting water and money, it can oversaturate your soil and promote disease. Denver afternoon storms can dump a lot of water quickly, and adding irrigation on top of that is pure waste. A rain sensor or smart controller with weather intelligence will pause your system automatically when it rains. It's a cheap upgrade that pays for itself fast. Ask us about rain sensors at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What time of day should I be watering my lawn?
faqs.answer: Water early in the morning, ideally finishing before 10 AM. Watering in the heat of the afternoon wastes a huge amount of water to evaporation, especially at Denver's altitude with our intense sun and low humidity. Watering in the evening is also a mistake because the grass stays wet all night, creating a perfect environment for fungal diseases. Morning watering lets the grass dry during the day while minimizing evaporation loss. If your controller isn't set to morning cycles, we can fix that at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: What happens if I skip annual sprinkler maintenance?
faqs.answer: Skipping annual maintenance is how small problems become expensive repairs. Heads gradually lose alignment, nozzles clog, seals wear out, and coverage patterns shift without you noticing until your water bill spikes or brown spots appear. A yearly checkup catches these issues early when they're cheap and easy to fix. It also keeps your backflow device tested and compliant with local codes. An annual tune-up is the best money you can spend on your system, so schedule yours at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: How do I know if my sprinkler heads are adjusted properly?
faqs.answer: Run each zone and watch for heads spraying onto sidewalks, driveways, fences, or your house instead of the lawn and beds. Also look for heads that aren't popping up fully, are tilted, or have an arc that doesn't match the area they're supposed to cover. Misadjusted heads waste water and create dry spots that are easy to miss from inside the house. A quick walk-through while your system runs once a month catches most problems. For a thorough adjustment, book a tune-up at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: Can I use any pipe or fittings for sprinkler repairs?
faqs.answer: No, and using the wrong materials is a common DIY mistake that leads to repeat failures. Most Denver residential systems use either Schedule 40 PVC or polyethylene (poly) pipe, and the fittings are not interchangeable between them. Using hardware store compression fittings where barbed fittings with clamps are needed, or mixing PVC cement types, creates weak joints that blow apart under pressure. Always match the existing pipe type and use irrigation-grade fittings. If you're unsure what your system uses, we can handle the repair correctly at https://5280sprinklers.com/.

faqs.question: Why should I know where my sprinkler system's shutoff valve is?
faqs.answer: If a pipe bursts or a valve gets stuck open, your shutoff valve is the only way to stop water from flooding your yard or basement until help arrives. Every homeowner should know where their irrigation shutoff is and test it at least once a year to make sure it actually turns. It's usually near the backflow device, in the basement, or in a utility closet. A stuck or hidden shutoff valve can turn a simple broken pipe into thousands of dollars in water damage. If you can't find yours, we'll locate and tag it for you at https://5280sprinklers.com/.
